utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Colonel Robert Franken served in the Royal Netherlands Army for 33 years retiring as a lieutenant-colonel. From January to July 1995, he was a major assigned to DutchBat in Potocari, where he was the deputy commanding officer and chief of logistics. He describes the impact of the increasingly strict restrictions placed by the VRS on DutchBat supply convoys leading up to the take-over of Srebrenica, including restrictions on spare parts, communications equipment, food, weapons, fuel, and DutchBat personnel. Colonel Franken describes events leading up to the VRS take-over of Srebrenica, including the attack on observation post, or OP Echo, on June 3rd and the attacks beginning on July 6th. On July 10th, the VRS issued an ultimatum demanding that civilians, BiH soldiers, DutchBat and UNHCR leave the enclave by 0600 on July 11th. By July 11th, most of the Dutch OPs had fallen and their DutchBat crews were taken prisoner. On the morning of the 12th of July, Serb forces entered Potocari. Sometime afternoon, a large number of buses and trucks began arriving and the transportation of the civilian population began. Colonel Franken ordered DutchBat officers to escort the first convoy but soon after the VRS blocked other UN escorts, stripping them of their weapons, equipment, and clothing. Colonel Franken describes the fear and desperate humanitarian conditions for the Muslims who had fled to Potocari. There were reports of executions of Muslim men. Men were separated and taken to the white house and then transported towards Bratunac. The Serbs blocked DutchBat efforts to enter the white house and blocked their efforts to escort those buses as well. Colonel Franken complained to VRS Colonel Jankovic, who told him the men at the white house were POWs. To provide some measure of protection to these men in the compound, Colonel Franken had a list created of some 250 names of the men. He informed Colonel Jankovic of the list. Later, Colonel Jankovic informed Colonel Franken of the ABiH breakout from the enclave and stated that the Serb forces already had 6.000 POWs. Colonel Franken also learned from one of his OP crews that they had seen a large group of men kneeling in rows on a soccer field with their hands on their necks. Lastly, on JUL 17th, Colonel Jankovic asked Colonel Franken and Mr. Nesib Mandzic to sign a document stating that the evacuations had been conducted according to international law. Colonel Franken added a proviso to neutralise such assertions and signed the document because doing so would facilitate the evacuation of wounded Bosnian Muslims. He describes as nonsense the document's assertion that the population could remain in the enclave. Your Honours, this concludes the summary of the witness's evidence. May I proceed with the questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sir, in your amalgamated statement, and I'm referring generally to paragraphs 22 to 31, you described the restrictions on Dutch resupply convoys in the hardship that created in the Srebrenica enclave for DutchBat. Since we have it there, I won't go over those issues in any detail. Rather, I'd like to focus on a few topics, taking first the fuel restrictions. And you state that the last fuel convoy came in February of 1995, and that's in paragraph 26. Would it be right that after that DutchBat still continued to request fuel resupply convoys?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just to remind the Chamber you explain, paragraph 29, that DutchBat needed 8.000 to 9.000 litres of fuel a day to do its job. In the period of March up to July 1995, how much fuel did DutchBat actually have to use per day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, we came down to amount of 250 litres of diesel a day for the complete battalion, including the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I would like to turn to a document that you've seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could please have 65 ter 05384 brought up on the screen. And -- yes, thank you. Now, we'll have the English up in a minute but if I could begin in the meanwhile. This is -- and there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This is a document from the 10th of March, 1995, and we can see that it's from the Main Staff for the VRS to the Drina Corps Command. I would like to turn specifically to page 3 of the English and paragraph 4 in particular, and I believe that would be on page 2 of the -- of the B/C/S in e-court. And I would like to direct your attention to approximately in the middle of that page, as you'll see under the word "note" the sentence: "We did not allow the following: Three fuel tankers and five trailer trucks." And further down, on the second -- after the second word -- second occasion of the word "note," there's a sentence that begins: "We did not allow 36 cubic metres of diesel fuel." Bearing in mind the date of this document, would this be consistent with the situation you've described in your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is. It is consistent with the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn then to the last page of this document in English. I'm sorry, the second-to-last page. That would be page 6. And that's the second page of the -- I'm sorry, the third page of the B/C/S. And I'd like to direct your attention specifically to the bottom paragraph where it states: "Discuss the information on unapproved convoys with check-points, do not tell third persons and do not give any explanation to UNPROFOR representatives (pretend you did not get them). If a convoy shows up at a crossing point, return it to the place of departure." My question to you, sir: Did your convoy drivers ever receive, in fact, any explanation as to the denials of resupply requests?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. My drivers did not, my convoy driver did not, neither did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You anticipated my follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So with that, Your Honours, I would tender 65 ter 05384 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05384 receives number P1418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, P1418 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to have another document brought up. This time 65 ter 05568.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document, as we can see, is a 15th of June, 1995, communication from the Main Staff, the VRS Main Staff, again to the command of the Drina Corps. If we could turn, please, to page 3 of the English which should also be page 3 of the B/C/S, if I'm not mistaken. We see at the bottom that the -- this document is signed -- or is under the signature block of Colonel Radivoje Miletic, who is stand-in Chief of Staff. That's a little bit -- that last word is a bit obscured by that English phrase draft translation. My question to you, if I could direct your attention to this last page where it states: "Check the level of fuel in tanks, add the necessary tool (a stick) ready for the checking, measure the level of fuel in the tanks at the entrance to the enclave and after. Carry out the checking and enable them to move along the above cited routes." Sir, do you know what this so-called checking of the level of the fuel in the tanks what is this a reference to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, they did check with a check literally how much fuel there was in the tanks of the vehicles coming in, so the tanks of the vehicle itself, and checked when they went out if there was still fuel in those tanks probably to prevent us from taking out fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And just so that, if I understand your answer correctly, if you could confirm for the Trial Chamber you say the fuel tanks of the trucks itself. These are not fuel tankers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Tanks for the vehicle itself to drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I would like to briefly turn back to the first page of this document. And in the -- on the right-hand side in the English translation, you'll see in the upper right-hand corner a reference that reads, "Security officers shall" -- I'm sorry. Let me read that line above that, "NO BP, which is chief of intelligence and security," and below that, "Security officers shall witness detailed control." And it is signed "M. Nikolic." Do you recall who this M. Nikolic is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I suppose that is our liaison of the VRS being a member of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall what the first name of this individual was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Momo or something like that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's okay. If you can't recall, I'll continue on. The -- my last question on this document, sir, this checking of the fuel tank with a stick, how long did that -- do you remember what time-period that went on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not really. It -- it combined, it started at a certain time, and I can't remember whether that it ended. I suppose they always did that after that, they started it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we've seen that document is, of course, is June 15th. If you remember, do you know if that checking with a stick in the fuel tank started before that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, not exactly. But around that date I heard that it was reported to me and I had a big laugh, but then it started, and I never had reports that it had been done before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could move on to the next document, please, and that would be 65 ter ... I'm sorry, thank you, Ms. Stewart. Can I -- the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 05568 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05568 receives number P1419, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1419 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask one question before we proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, you explained that checking would serve the purpose of verifying whether no fuel was taken out of the compound -- was taken out of the enclave. Now, is that ... or did I misunderstand your ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tried to say that the checking was just that we didn't take any fuel from the vehicles who came in as a convoy vehicle. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me check. Then I have misunderstood you and there is no need to put me question. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And thank you, Witness, for the clarification. Actually just before we move on to the next -- actually, if I could ask -- if I could have the next document brought up. That's 65 ter 05351. And perhaps while we're waiting for that document to come up, sir, just -- just incidentally you had mentioned that DutchBat required 8.000 to 9.000 litres of fuel per day to operate. Realistically, how much fuel, if it ever happened, would DutchBat be able to take out of the fuel tank of convoy trucks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, all together, let's say when it was a bigger convoy there were about ten vehicles. We're talking about 150 or 200 litres diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now we have this document up and we see that it is again a document from the Main Staff of the VRS on the first page at the top dated 18th of June 1995. On the right-hand side of the top we see that it is sent to a number of brigades. If I could briefly turn to the second page of this document, please. And we see that it is also signed by Colonel Radivoje Miletic, who, as indicated in the signature block, is standing in for the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If -- I'm sorry, I think I had stated that it was signed, but that may -- there's a handwritten note about the standing in for the Chief of Staff. But perhaps it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, it seems that at least the name appears. Whether that is as a signature or just written is -- perhaps you could compare with the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if we -- I would like to direct your attention to the first page of this document. And going to -- under paragraph 3, several lines down from -- from that, the beginning of paragraph, there's a line that begins: "Cargo for Srebrenica: One container with eight pallets of frozen food, one container with eight pallets of dry food, and one tanker with 11 cubic metres of diesel fuel." Now we saw that this document is dated the 18th of June, 1995. You had explained that your last fuel convoy into -- for DutchBat was in February. So I'd like to ask you: Do you recall receiving this 11 cubic metres of diesel fuel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. And if it happened I'm sure that I would recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to turn your attention to a little further down in that paragraph, the line beginning -- or the line that reads: "I demand a detailed check of all vehicles including the inspection of cargo. Pay special attention to the fuel in the fuel tanks and the fuel being brought into the enclaves."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be a problem with e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It's at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see there's a difference between the left and the right screen we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- I'm not blaming you for anything at this moment. Let me see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: LiveNote the record is moving, but it's stopped in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On page 14, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that this is then a problem for the technicians. Because transcription is made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, meanwhile, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least on the left screen we still have the transcription. The only problem is that we can't move through it. But apart from that, the inconvenience is such that we can meanwhile continue, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I may have been a little ahead of myself. But my apology, it was directed to the fact that I think we should be on the second page of the B/C/S for that last quote that I'd read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not yet working, but ... I think it's working now. You may have to reconnect, but mine is functioning again. And, again, by reconnecting, it should be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can continue, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just to reiterate I believe for that last quote I read which is page 1 of the English in e-court we should actually be on page 2 of the B/C/S in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sir, the -- the last quote I had read related to -- this issue of pay special attention to the fuel in the fuel tanks and my question for you is whether this reference that I've just read, is this the same issue that you explained earlier about checking with the stick in the fuel tanks to see if DutchBat has taken any fuel from the convoy trucks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that, I would tender 65 ter 5351 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05351 receives number P1420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1420 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Colonel Franken, you explained in your statement, and that would be in paragraph 29 and elsewhere, that fuel shortages caused DutchBat to rely on foot patrols rather than vehicles. You also described in your statement, paragraph 29, the impact of fuel shortages on food, water, medical services, and heating. So I won't go through all that again since the Trial Chamber has your evidence. But I'd like to focus on this issue of medical services. Could you explain how it was that fuel shortages had an impact on medical services?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had a hospital in the compound and that needed energy, energy for cooling supplies, energy to keep the operations room operational, et cetera, et cetera. And the only source of energy we had was fuel because there was no energy source in the enclave whatsoever. So all energy we needed for all our jobs came from the diesel that was meant for generators, so we had electric - electricity, I mean - and the dressing station, the hospital needed electricity to keep their -- to keep functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And I think that's clear. But just to be sure, DutchBat, did it have any other source of electricity apart from what was produced by these generators?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In -- as I mentioned, you -- did you discuss the impact of fuel shortages going well beyond vehicles? Let me ask you this: What impact, if any, did it have on the weapons readiness, if I could uses that phrase, of DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your -- your question. The lack of energy was not directly diminishing our weapons capacities because that was all mechanical. Lack of fuel did have impact on a maintenance, et cetera, of course, but not on the weapons system itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And following on that, this maintenance aspect, was there an issue that related to moisture in some of your ordnance or ammunition?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- I probably misunderstood your first question. But fact is that, for instance, the -- the -- the ammunition for our TOW, and the TOW is an anti-tank system, there are rockets in that and they have to be kept quite dry. We had a sea container with a device in it to dry the air and there were the rockets for the TOWs stored. But to a -- in a certain stage we came that far that we couldn't afford energy to dry our rockets, which meant that the rockets and mortar, ammunition, and things like that were not operational anymore because they were spoiled by moisture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And staying on this issue of ammunition and weapons related issues, you describe in your statement, that would be paragraph 30, the impact of the convoy restrictions on various weapons and weapons systems. So, again, I won't go through that. I'd like to focus your attention, though, to one aspect of your paragraph 30 where you discuss that the average supplies of ammunition was at 16 per cent. First, just to be clear, does that mean only 16 per cent of DutchBat ammunition supplies were available for use?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. If you total it, that is correct. We had 16 per cent of the total amount of ammunition we should have. But then again, that 16 per cent is a bit puzzling because it counted it all together. It meant that for specific ammunitions like anti-tank ammunition, I was down to zero. But the system of UN reporting they wanted to know the total amount in numbers and then they said, You have that number so that means 16 per cent. But it doesn't really give a good picture of -- of the ammunition stores we had. For instance, I had -- I had about 30 per cent of my small-calibre ammunition, meaning for the guns, the rifles of the soldiers, but my mortar ammunition was down to, yeah, approximately 10 and my anti-tank ammunition was practically zero. So 16 per cent gives a strange -- it's a strange way to report things but that is the actually situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Sir, can you say, based on your knowledge, whether the VRS would have known the impact of the convoy restrictions on DutchBat operational effectiveness?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And how can you say that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the weapons systems we had were -- were known to the VRS, technically as well. They knew exactly what came in and they controlled that. So they could make an estimation of our stocks. A nice example is we tried to get in testing equipment for the TOW. Well, just to make that clear, every time you start up the TOW system you have to do a check with some kind of a computer, check some things, and then it's operational. That machine broke down and we tried to get in a new one. But the VRS wouldn't let us which indicates that they really knew what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in this particular case, you're talking about this testing system. Would -- would it be -- in the same vein would it be right that other resupply requests you made also indicated what DutchBat basically needed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've been discussing the convoy restrictions and it's in your statement relating to the fuel, food, troop rotations and equipment. What was the impact of all this on DutchBat morale, if any?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Of course, it had impact on the morale of my soldiers. To give an idea, they didn't get post from home, which is very important when you're in an isolated situation like that. They didn't go on leaves because they were not allowed to rotate. We had a one -- every week we had a two-minute shower for every of our soldiers, which is very little seeing the circumstances. And if you can't keep clean that's not good for morale as well. Food was during weeks only combat rations, never fresh food. We had even a period of about ten days or seven days that we had a menu of in the morning for breakfast rice and peanut butter, for lurch peanut butter and rise, and as dinner peanut butter and rice combination. And things like that are not good for morale. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And again, based on your own knowledge, is this something that military officer, including military officers of the VRS that they would know was an impact on DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to a different topic now, moving to the 9th of July. In your amalgamated statement, paragraph 52, Your Honours, you explain that DutchBat received an order to defend Srebrenica with all -- all military means. You then describe issuing an operational order which is also referred to as a green order, I believe, which you explain in your statement was conveying to Captain Groen that he could immediately use all his means without the restrictions of the UN to execute this order. Now, my question for you at this stage is: How would you characterise what "all of DutchBat's military means" realistically meant at this time, bearing in mind what you've just described about the impact of the convoy restrictions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sounds good, but in fact it meant that there were no restrictions on weapon use. Only problem was, of course, he had mortars but hardly any ammunition for it. Of course, he should have anti-tank systems, not operational. But just to make sure for him that if he wanted to use the little mortar ammunition he had he was free to do so because there were all kinds of restrictions within the mandate of using weapons systems. And I tried to make clear to him that those restrictions were gone within the -- this defence order for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the operational order or green order itself. If I could please have 65 ter 05278 up on the screen. Colonel Franken, we're bringing up the -- probably the English and B/C/S versions. The Dutch is also available. If you would like to refer to that at any point, please just indicate so. While we're waiting for that, sir, this is a document that you have seen before. It's -- as we can see it's from you to Captain Groen. Actually if you could just clarify for us, we see across the top in fact that there are several dates and times on this document. But would it be correct that in the third -- more or less the third line, this reference to 9th of July, 1995, would that be the correct date? And 1952 hours, would that be the correct time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the correct time, as far as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, by correct time I mean the actual time of transmission of this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, if I can direct your attention we see about two-thirds of the way down the page, and I believe in the B/C/S that would be around in the middle of that -- of this page, we see the following letters, "N. B." And then we see, "This is a seriously intended green assignment." If we look above, the contents of what -- of the assignment seem to be laid out; namely, "Preparation and arrangement of defence of the southern edge of Srebrenica." And then there follows some directional guidance. And then the document states, "Prevent with all available means a break-through of the BSA into the town." First, are we reading this document correctly that this paragraph that begins with the word "assignment" that this constitutes the green assignment or the green order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, what we've just seen there -- are -- is this defensive action and this preventative action that that is what is ordered. In seeing that, how should we understand the actually implementation of the green order concept in the situation facing DutchBat in 9th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: At first, there are no two phases. In fact, his order is to defend the city, and the aim of the defence is to prevent the BSA entering the town. I won't give you a tactical lessons but you can have another type of defence. But here it was: Stop him before he enters town. Which includes: When he enters town, hit him out. That's first. And just to read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Implementation of the green concept, well -- well, that's [indiscernible] before, but the point is we were an elite unit trained for air assault. So we were trained pretty aggressively with full use of our weapon systems. Then we had to go to Bosnia, we got UN training. In that training, we had to bring down the aggressive feelings of our soldiers. We have to cool them down. We had to make policemen of them and not elite soldiers anymore. And during that training, we used -- that is blue training. Blue refers to the UN colours, blue helmet, et cetera. And if we did anything, we said, No, this is green, which was meant normal operations, military operations. So there is the green and the blue words coming from. To make sure for him that it is an assignment the defence like in Germany against former Warsaw Pact or something like that. That's why I noted again, I put that note under it. It is a seriously intended green assignment to get his nose in a direction, or his mind in the direction, No, UN, I'm not a policeman anymore, I'm a soldier now and I have to defend the town. You understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And just, again, you've described the green order as using all military means --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- without UN restrictions, at least the green order in concept, but is actually, as we see here, is actually applied. Given the limitations that you've described of DutchBat, what did -- all these military means, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, he could rely on his machine-guns and rifles, point. If you mean all military means in actually that is all he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would tender 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, can I have a question on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the document is dated 9th July 1995. My question to you, Mr. Franken, is: What is the significance of the date 12th September 1995 at the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see they are received from Captain Hageman, so I suppose that the source of this document where it came from, received that from Captain Hageman, who was the commander of the blocking positions out of his personal possession on the 12th September 1995. It is not -- that's what I suppose that happened. It is not really has anything to do with the document and the dates on the document itself. I think whoever had this or got this, got it from Captain Hageman and it was sent to them, or to him, on the 12 September 1995 when we were back in Holland quite some while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The English version disappeared from the screen. Perhaps we can have the Dutch version on the screen to see what is written -- what is typed and what is in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was going to be my very suggestion so we could see whether it is, in fact, handwritten across the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps meanwhile could the witness already answer the following question. Was there a Team 7 or was there a Team J?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Team 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at the Dutch version as soon as it comes up on the screen, it says in handwriting "received from Captain Hageman, 12th September 1995." Therefore, we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I see "ploeg," which is -- the Dutch is translated as "team." And then something appears which, as far as I can decipher, could be either a 7 or a J. Are you aware of any J team or a 7 team?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the top of that page, please, in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see what you mean and I only can guess. In that period, September 1995, there was a Dutch debriefing of DutchBat. The interrogators or the debriefers were organised in teams. So I suppose that it is Team 7 of the Dutch debriefing team. It's not a unit or a part of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then your understanding would be that that debriefing team would have received this document from Captain Hageman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct, sir -- Your Honour, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tendered it, Mr. Shin. No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5278 receives number P1421.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1421 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move now to the events in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July and focus first -- my first questions on what you identify as the white house. Now, you describe in your amalgamated statement, that would be paragraph 86, that Muslim men were being brought there to a house, to this White house, which you and others have identified, and that this white house was about 150 metres from the entrance to the DutchBat compound. If I could please have 65 ter 17875 brought up on the screen. Now, while we're waiting for that to come up, Colonel Franken, what we'll see is an aerial image of the Potocari area around the DutchBat compound and this is an aerial image that you will recall you marked during your testimony in the Popovic case. If we could just have that enlarged I'll just ask you to orient yourself for a minute, and we see in the upper right-hand corner an arrow with the letter N indicating, presumably, the direction north?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we can see there you have marked around the middle of the document, a little bit to the left, the word white house. Just so that we're clear that's the indication of that house. My question to you sir: Did you go to the white house yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How -- how close did you get to the white house?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it's 80 metres, 80, 90 metres just the beginning of the road to the white house coming from the road Bratunac-Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you personally see the Bosnian Muslim men who were being led there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that there were columns of men brought to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you able to see who it was who was leading those men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, they were brought there by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And were -- just so that we're clear, when you say "Bosnian Serbs," were these Bosnian Serbs in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: While we have this map up, could you just explain to the Trial Chamber what this dotted line is that we see in the middle going roughly in a north/south direction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: During the events, I gave order to Major Otter, being the base commander, to prepare a safe route for the refugees to come into the compound. Why that, the area you see on the photograph, say, left of our UN base, was completely inside of Serbian artillery. And they used that gun oftenly, so I want to prevent that when the refugees came to our base, they came under fire of that Serb artillery. So we had to recon, to recon I should say, a route which gave cover to that artillery and the dotted line is approximately the result of that recon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to be clear, when you say that area to the left was completely -- left of the UN base was completely inside of Serbian artillery would it be right that you mean they are within range or [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in range anyway, but there was line of sight from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again ask you to make short breaks between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please resume. Perhaps we could -- I think the question was whether it would be right that it was in range of the Serb artillery. And then could you re-start your answer there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was not only within range but it was in direct sight of a gun positions directly north of Observation Post Papa on a reach. And that gun was used frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You state in your -- in your amalgamated statement, paragraph 89, you state that you informed Colonel Jankovic about the situation of the Muslim men being taken to the white house. Do you recall what it was that you told him about that situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not exactly. But -- but the meeting was that I got reports that the -- the treating of the men got worse and in some kind of phrase I made him clear that it was incorrect. He had to do something about it. And as I recollect he said, Well, okay I'll see to it or -- and then he emphasised again that he in fact had nothing to do with the evacuation, et cetera, that he was only there to prepare the withdrawal of the DutchBat itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in your statement, you also explained that Colonel -- this is paragraph 89 again, Your Honours, that Colonel Jankovic had told you that these men were POWs --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- and that if the Serb soldiers were being too aggressive he would take steps to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection were you aware of any steps that were take [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't know whether he took any steps but I didn't see any results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 17875 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Aerial marked by the witness in a previous case. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17875 receives number P1422, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1422 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask one additional question, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, you said that you were not at the white house but you saw columns of men taken there. Do you remember what they were wearing and whether they were carrying any arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the men going in were civil or a combination of civil and military clothing. Quite a lot of them still had bags or -- or things like that with them and they went in a column to the house and I could even see some men on the balcony of the white house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was about arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether they were carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Muslims were not carrying arms, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, you -- the picture of men being dressed in civilian or in a combination of civil and military clothing, was it that all of them had this mixed clothing or a small part of them, or -- could you further elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men I saw then, a part of them had, for instance, camouflage trousers or things like that and the rest of them were in civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the approximate percentage was of persons which were mixed. Was that a majority or was that a minority or was it a small minority? Could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand your question. So the party I saw it was a minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, 45 to 55 is a minority; 20 to 80 is a minority as well. Could you any further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to give figures. The group I saw was approximately 30 up till 40 men in total, and I think 10 up to 15 were combinations of civil and military clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a short follow-up question. You said, I quote: "Quite a lot of them still had bags or things like that with them." What did they do with these bags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, later on, it proved that those bags and rucksacks, et cetera, were piled at the -- quite close to the road, Bratunac-Srebrenica, say about 70 metres in front of the white house, and later they set fire on that. They, I mean, the VRS set fire on those Muslim belongings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, I'm looking at the clock. We'll take a break of 20 minutes. Mr. Shin, are you on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break, but not until after Mr. Franken has left the courtroom. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, while waiting for the witness to come in, could I please have the next document brought up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That would be 65 ter 05142.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Colonel Franken, just before we took the break, you heard His Honour Judge Fluegge's question regarding the burning of the bags and other materials that you saw in front of the white house. I am -- I've asked for an image to be brought up on the screen. And you will recall in your amalgamated statement and paragraph 100, Your Honours, you do address this picture. Do you recognise this -- these two pictures, these two photographs, in fact, as images showing that burning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 05142 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05142 receives number P1423, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1432 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic indicated there were no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, continuing on with the situation in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July, in your statement at paragraphs 94 and 95, you discuss two reported executions in Potocari the first of these was a discovery of nine bodies in the -- behind the area of the white house and that was reported to you by Lieutenant-Colonel Koster himself. That is in paragraphs 94 and 95. Just so that we're clear, was it Lieutenant-Colonel Koster himself who saw those bodies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Just for the record, it is a Lieutenant Koster not lieutenant-colonel Koster in the transcript. But that is correct. Koster was there himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the Chamber may recall hearing some evidence on this last July. Colonel Franken, I'd like to ask you about the second report of an execution which you address in your statement and that's also in those two paragraphs. This is -- this involved a single -- a one -- one person who was executed in this instance and you explained that it was reported to you by a DutchBat soldier -- I'm sorry, that it was reported to you that a DutchBat soldier from Charlie Company had witnessed the execution. My question to you is: Do you recall -- if you can, do you recall of that soldier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, well, Groenewegen, Groenewelt. Well, sorry, no I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. How was this -- how was that information reported to you? Was it like Lieutenant Koster by the witness himself or was it through another channel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I understood, a soldier reported that to his company commander Captain Matthijssen, company C, and the company commander reported that to the Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans. And as far as I recollect I heard it from Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, so it was not reported directly to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to turn briefly now back to the situation, the take-over of DutchBat OPs. This is set out in some detail in your statement, mostly paragraphs 38 through 51 but also in 58 through 59, so I won't be going through most of that. What I'd like to focus your attention on is the crew of OP Alpha. You explain in paragraph 99 that they were brought back to the enclave. Unlike the other crews they were not taken prisoner in Bratunac. And you state -- you explain in your statement that they reported to you that on their way back to Potocari, they saw a big group of men kneeling in a soccer field. If you can, could you -- if you can, can you describe to the Trial Chamber what this means, the big group? How many are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't get a number but it said a massive group so I can't give numbers. And as far as I recollect those men were on their knees with their hands in their neck in rows in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the best that you can recall, do you know what place that was where your men saw this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The exact place I do not know. I only can deduce it was on the route from the military area to Bratunac because that's the route they followed when they were brought back. So somewhere along that route, that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin paragraph 99 starts with, "After the 13th of July," which is a rather vague reference as far as time is concerned. It's reads: "After 13th July when the crew of Observation Post Alpha was brought back over a road north of the enclave." Is there a mistake or could you clarify that with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard His Honour's question. The paragraph 99 in your statement begins after 13th of July, is that correct? Or to the best of your recollection when did the -- first of all, when did the screw of OP Alpha get back to Potocari, and secondly, to the best of your recollection, when did the crew from OP Alpha see the men in the field?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: To answer the last question, they saw it during their move back to the camp. But as far as I recollect, I'm not sure it was in the end of the 13th of July or in the morning of the 14th, that they actually came back. But, I'm sorry, I don't exactly know anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. But if --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Time-period, let's say between 13th of July, 1800, somewhere up until the 14th early in the morning. 1100. Somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you've just explained that that's the time that they came back. When would it be that they saw these men kneeling in the field. When would it be that these men were kneeling in the field?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It would be a guess. Seeing the distance and they were brought in with one of my own trucks because the VRS asked me to give them a truck and a driver to pick up the crew of OP Alpha, I figure they had a time -- they needed to move from Alpha on that route to Potocari will be an hour, hour and a half, seeing the condition of the roads. So, yeah, during that move, they saw it. But I can't connect an exact timing on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, which day are we talking about then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, as I told you, to my recollection, now it was the end of the 13th. But I'm not sure. It could have been the morning of the 14th as well. I'm very sorry, but it's long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'd like to move on to a list that you had made of names of Bosnian Muslim men inside the compound at Potocari. You describe in your statement, paragraphs 90, 91, various aspects of how this list was made so I won't go through that. Bu could you explain to this Court what your motivation was. Why was it you believed that it was important to create this list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, as I stated before, we saw the handling of the men in the white house getting worse. I tried to get patrols over there to do something in which I did not succeed. So I tried to find out a way to give them some more protection. And then I remembered that, as far as I know, a NGO did in a similar situation he gave the man an identity by making a list, trying to get photographs, et cetera, and make it public that things were happening. That's exactly what I meant with it. My idea was, Okay, give them a name, make a list, make to the out world clear that 251 men, not anonymous but with names and ages, et cetera, are in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs. And that's why I decided to send it to every higher level I had in that time, with the request to publish it or to make it known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also state in paragraph -- in your statement that would be paragraph 112, that in due course you had an opportunity to tell Colonel Jankovic about this list. Do you recall whether Colonel Jankovic said anything in response when you explained to him --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- this list.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was no reaction, took it for granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court when it was, to the best of your recollection, that you told Colonel Jankovic about this list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, just digging in my memory. It would have been on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And approximately what time on the 13th, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, Mr. Franken, could I ask you again not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Colonel Franken, that is my fault. I will take care to pause between the question and the answer. If you would follow likewise I think we should be good.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I will try my best again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now you also indicate in your statement that later after you'd told Colonel Jankovic about this list, that Colonel Jankovic informed you about the breakout of the 28th Division, and just so we're clear this is the ABiH 28th Division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And by break out, again just to be clear, that's breaking out from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In paragraph 112, you also state that Colonel Jankovic told you that they already had 6.000 POWs. Can you tell this Chamber with as much precision as possible when it was that you recall he told you that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The end of the 13th, it must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear when you told you they had 6.000 POWs, that's obviously the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to move now to your meeting on the 17th of July with delegation headed by again -- in this -- once again this individual had you met before, Colonel Jankovic. You explain in paragraph 105 of your statement that the part of the document stating that the population can remain in the enclave or evacuate. You use the word "nonsense" in your statement to describe that. And you explained that the population did not have a "realistic opportunity" to stay and that "they did not have a choice." Now my question to you, sir, this may be obvious, this may have been obvious to you in that place and at that time, but could you please explain to the Trial Chamber today why concretely you believed there was no realistic opportunity or choice to stay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Then I'll have to describe shortly the situation the population was in. Weather 30, 35 degrees centigrade, no water, no food, bad hygienic situation. The people were exhausted. When they stayed -- well, the choice. There was theoretically a choice. The choice is in being crowded in weather like that with no supplies, with no food, with no medical care comes to the fact then die slowly or get out. If you call that a choice, they had a choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Colonel Franken, continuing in that vein you mention elsewhere in your statement, and, Your Honours, I'm referring to paragraph 80, when you describe the transportation of the population out of Potocari, you used the word -- that they voluntarily got on the buses. At the same time, you explained that they had no other choice, no alternative. In the same vein, was the choice that you just outlined between dying slowly or getting out, was that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's what I meant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Turning back briefly to this 17th of July statement, if I could please have -- it's -- it's -- it's in evidence already. If I could please have on the screen P1138 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1118"] just for reference during the witness's testimony. Colonel Franken, as you explain in your statement you added a provision, handwritten, to the end of this declaration that's reads: "As far as convoys actually escorted by UN forces are concerned..." And while we're waiting for this document to come up, and we see that on the very bottom of the -- of the text. Could you -- in your statement you explain that you by including this phrase you wanted to neutralise this whole statement. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was known that we did not actually or effectively could escort the -- the -- the convoys and by adding this phrase into my opinion, I neutralised or I gave that declaration no further meaning, no content in fact. Because, in the end I said, Yeah, could have been. But we couldn't see that or we can't confirm that because we were not able to really control the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And given the explanations you've just provided to this Trial Chamber, could you explain to them also why it was -- given your understanding of this document, your perception of this document, why it was that you signed it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, Colonel Jankovic made in a -- in a way clear to me that it would be -- what do you say. That it would be good for -- for -- for the -- the -- the -- the transport of the 59 wounded, that it would make that easier when this -- this declaration was signed. He had not said that it was a condition, but it would -- what do you say. Sorry. It would be -- it would positively influence the -- the transport of the wounded. I think that's the best thing I can make of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, I see on the transcript it reads that P1118 was called and we're talking about P1138.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies, Your Honour. That is correct. It is 1138. I certainly had that written down, so I'm sorry if I misread that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least there is a problem in the transcript and it has been corrected now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The last document that I'd like to show you, Colonel Franken, if I could please have -- well, let me say this is a document that you were not shown by me but I believe you were shown in your Karadzic testimony. This is a document that's in evidence. It's under seal. So if we could have it brought up on the screen but not transmitted. It's P1235.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I just quickly explain, Your Honours, that we had this on our list of potential additional exhibits as 65 ter -- under a different 65 ter number, but the two documents are identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And on your list appeared what document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It would be 20939A. And the original 65 ter number of the admitted document would be 20939B. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Colonel Franken, if you could please read this. It's -- it's very brief. If you could just read this intercept document. If could you just signal when you've had a chance to do so.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We see near the top in that first paragraph that the letter M is indicated as General Mladic speaking. And in the second line, he is asking: "Have these buses and trucks left?" Now further down, we see the quote: "They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to." And this is again indicated as being stated by General Mladic. Now this sentiment that all those will be evacuated who want to and those who don't want to, is this consistent with the reality of what you saw in terms of the real choice or opportunity to remain in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I said, in fact, they didn't have a choice, and, well, this is consistent with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour -- Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions at this stage by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's already in evidence. Yes, you told us before. Before I give an opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness, I have a few questions. I don't know, Mr. Franken, you don't have a hard copy of your statement before you. Is any of the parties -- we could also have it on the screen. I'm looking for paragraphs 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Officer, the statement to be provided to Colonel Franken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I start with paragraph 12. Mr. Franken, paragraph 12 starts with the following words: "The contacts to the Bosnian Serb army were through the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, Ramiz." Is that what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's incorrect, sir. It would have been very nice when the situation was like that, we wouldn't have a situation there. But it is incorrect. The Chief of Staff 28th Division, the 28th Division is a Muslim division, and it should be that the contact to the Bosnian Serb army were through Major Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade. I indicated that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or it should be in view of what then follows, the contact to the BiH army were through because the follow-up is all about the context, I'd say with the 28th Division and with Mr. Oric. So that is then corrected hereby and understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'd like to take you back also to paragraph 11. You said: "The problem was that in fact there were three confrontation line, three borders of the enclave. There was an UN border, a Bosnian Serb border, more or less 1 or 2 kilometres further within the enclave, and the Muslim border, which was locally 1 or 2 kilometres further outside the UN border." Now if I try to imagine for myself that what happens, you have a separation line, an UN separation line, and then the Bosnian Serbs 2 kilometres further within, and the Muslims 2 kilometres further out, which gives a -- I just have difficulties in fully understanding how that works because there would be an overlap of 4 kilometres in which there were both Bosnian Serb and ABiH forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would have been 4 kilometres when that difference was on the same spot, Your Honour. For instance, in the south, in the area of Zeleni Jadar, the Bosnian Serbs claimed that the border was including OP Echo, and the ABiH claimed that the border was further south -- sorry, yeah, farther south of Zeleni Jadar and there the difference was about 800 metres. The 2 kilometres referred to the maximum difference in opinion, but it was never on the same spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, as a matter of fact, there was dispute about where the separation lines between the armies should be more inside or more outside of the enclave, according to the UN --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- borders. That is how we have to understand it. That's clear to me now. Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready to cross-examine the witness, you may proceed. Mr. Franken -- and by the way, I address you as Mr. Franken and not by title or rank. That is a habit in this courtroom just to call everyone mister or madam. Mr. Stojanovic will now cross-examine you. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Franken. I'm also going to address you in that same way. Please don't feel offended because that is our usual practice. Let us start with the last topic discussed a while ago, and His Honour pointed out to the three separation lines in paragraph 11. Would you agree with me that the very fact that there was no accurate delineation or that there were no identical interpretation of the separation line was a latent cause of dispute between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as your first mark is there was an accurate delineation. For us, it was the UN border. And for the interpretation of the line and the cause of dispute, I can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us first address a topic that has already been tackled and that is the UNPROFOR mandate in the Srebrenica demilitarised zone. Before January 1995, did you have any information about what your specific duties would be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. The order -- the assignment we had from the UN was known to me before I came to Bosnia; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it derive from the cease-fire agreement in the territory of the enclave concluded between General Ratko Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic on the 8th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know the exact text of that -- that agreement, but as far as I know, it did not derive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please first look at those documents and then I'm going to ask you how you perceived your mandate. And for that purpose, can we please call up P23 in e-court. Please look at paragraph 3, 4, and 5. Can we please have paragraphs 3, 4, and 5. Mr. Franken, in paragraph 3 of this agreement, there is mention of demilitarisation, and deadlines are set for the surrender of weapons by the parties. In paragraph 5, it is stated what UNPROFOR is supposed to do. And it also says, in passage 3 of paragraph 5, that in order for it to be able to carry out the rotation and other jobs relating to units would have the freedom of movement outside of the demilitarised zone. And in the next paragraph, it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're invited to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you: "Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone, except members or UNPROFOR, are not permitted to have in their possession any weapon, ammunition, or explosives. Weapons, ammunition or explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR." And the last passage reads: "Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that precisely your mandate, among other things?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was. We had orders to demilitarise the zone, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We can agree that at the time when you arrived there in January 1995 the zone was not demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The weapons and artillery pieces handed over prior to your arrival, in the course of the initial implementation of the agreement, was negligible, in terms of the quality and in terms of quantity, and in terms of the level of state of the art of weapons concerned.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Is that a question or a statement, sir? If you want me to confirm, I could confirm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I just wanted you to confirm this. Will you agree with me that neither the DutchBat, during their mandate, failed, despite their good will, to disarm the elements of the 28th Division deployed inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I have to admit that we failed in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, we're going to discuss later the so-called green order. Can you tell me now whether, according to this agreement and its language, can you tell us if you can see here a basis for the green order and the possibility, so to speak, of siding with one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. In the agreement, there is not a basis for the green order. That is stated before. The very moment that order came to defend the city, we concluded that our mandate had changed. And the possibility of siding with one of the warring parties, no, the mandate didn't give that. We can discuss whether it took place, but, in fact, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the entity that could have altered your mandate unilaterally without consultations with the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Simple. My next echelon, my higher command being BH command or Sector North-East.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was such an order altering your mandate that gave rise to the green order, did it arrive from north-east headquarters in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The order to defend the city of Srebrenica came from BH Command, BH Command being the command of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it conveyed through usual channels, BH Command, north-east Command, Sarajevo-Tuzla, Tuzla DutchBat or was it transferred directly from Sarajevo to the DutchBat? Altering your mandate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As in fact as I remember, it came directly down from BH Command, and in the text there was not a remark about altering my mandate but there was a discussion that the mission to defend would be impossible within the existing mandate. And as far as I heard from Colonel Karremans the remark was, Well, you've got to defend the city, point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the alteration of your mandate occur and when Colonel Karremans received an instruction to apply the green order and I also involve there the DutchBat as well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Again, the alteration of the mandate was implicit to the order to defend, and we got that order on the 9th of July. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you is that I'm puzzled by something in document P1421. And, Your Honours, if we can please have a brief look at that document. You will remember that that document was referred to in examination-in-chief and that it is dated the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Stojanovic, I will have a question on this document that's on the screen. I just wanted to ask Mr. Franken, Mr. Franken, when you got to Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you -- your mandate derived from this document, or did it derive from the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got into Bosnia it was DutchBat III, there was a written operational order in which our task was mentioned. And to be brief about that, we had the order to deter any aggression by presence, facilitate humanitarian aid, and -- well, that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. Is that document that you're talking about, is it this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. This is an agreement. We didn't get that agreement. We had a written military order from the UN, probably being BH command, in which our tasks were described. And our mission was, as I said, to deter by presence, facilitate humanitarian aid, and the third thing, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean this agreement, sir, I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Until today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until today, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for document P1421, I'd like to ask you this, Mr. Franken. Are you aware of the existence of such a written order relating to your mandate somewhere in archives whether it be of the DutchBat or somewhere in Sarajevo? Did you have this piece of paper in your hands at any point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you mean such a written order, and you mean the order to defend the city of Srebrenica, I had that in my hand, that is correct, on location. And whether it is in some archive or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was interested in the order that you spoke in response to His Honour Judge Moloto's question, and that concerned your mandate.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: You mean the initial order we had when we came in the -- the enclave. Yeah, I saw that order, of course, because we made an order for our battalion based on that order. I don't have that anymore, and whether it's in any archive or not, I suppose it is, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just intervene for a short moment. It's not the first time now that we're dealing with this agreement between the parties, the demilitarization agreement. I'm seeking the input of the parties on the following question. In the beginning of this document, it says that the demilitarised zone should be announced by -- by announcements. Demilitarised zone, Article 60 of the -- of Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions. Is it the view of the parties that, apart from what is agreed there, that the demilitarised zone is governed by Article 60 of Protocol I? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, speaking for the Prosecution, we would request a little bit of time to consider that before coming back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, then you would like to have additional time as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a starting point, and I would have preferred that we don't have to discuss any of this provided we can all agree on the issue of demilitarization and everything else, and I that would facilitate matters greatly, but I think this will have to be discussed with three or four more upcoming witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we have to ask witnesses about these legal issues, because they've never said anything about it. So, therefore, I wonder whether we need -- there's an old Latin saying that the Court knows the law and, of course, the Court is always assisted by the parties in getting full knowledge of the law. And whether we need witnesses for that is a different matter. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure if I understood entirely what Mr. Stojanovic was saying but if his position on -- is that the enclave was suppose to be demilitarised, well, yes we do agree that that was supposed to have happened. On a question of law, as I indicated if that is a matter we would like some time to come back to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to that, I would also like to hear the view of the parties on what their position is in view of the validity of this agreement in 1995, whether it applies or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We will discuss that issue as well and revert to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps you pay specific attention to Article 60, paragraph 7, of Protocol I. Meanwhile, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, let us look again at document P1421. I understood when you said that the order altering your -- your mandate you received on the 9th of July and that was directly from the Command in Sarajevo. But what confuses me is that there is a sentence in this document which reads that this is a seriously planned covert task. Prior to the moment when your mandate was changed, did you review or discuss such an option? That means becoming involved in active combat operations, which is something that is contained in the green order.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As first remark, I can't read in the document where it says that it is a seriously planned covert task, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may help you, it's somewhere in the middle of the English text, when you see N. B. And there were the sentence that I quoted is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No the quote is incomplete. I think it was not a covert task. It was: "This is a seriously intended green assignment." Is that what you wanted to refer to, Mr. Stojanovic? Or is there anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. There -- it may be there is an error in the translation in the B/C/S version. The -- our interpreters booth can perhaps correct us on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, usually the interpreters are not there to perform translation or -- but if they could help us out just for a second whether what we see in the B/C/S version of this document, as it appears on our screen at this moment, whether that reflects in B/C/S the English N. B, "this is a seriously intended green assignment."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
