utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The word "tajni" which means "secret" or "covert" was added in the translation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently something has been added into the translation and I think that the English seems to be, to me, a -- an accurate translation of the original Dutch version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may also I fully understand that this is not what the interpreters' booths are for. But just on this issue in addition to the addition of the word in the B/C/S translation that was cited it may be that there is a word missing. If the interpreters' booths could please alert us to that, and the specific word I'm thinking of is "green."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if we commit ourselves to not to ask again for their services as correcting translations. We need anyhow a corrected translation. We have to ask for that. But if the interpreters could help us out for this very moment that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There's no word "green" in the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the word "tajni" shouldn't be there. The word "green" should be there. Mr. Stojanovic, is it clear enough for you at this moment? Then the Prosecution is invited to take care that the new accurate translation will be attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, as soon as we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps it is possible to have the Dutch version on the screen again, and Mr. Franken can explain the original Dutch text to the Court and the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The translation from the Dutch document to the English document is correct. It's literally what it says in Dutch: A seriously intended, or meant, green assignment. So that translation is correct. It covers the -- the -- the meaning of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I read the word in the B/C/S. There is no word "secret," so we clarified that. But let me ask you this: Would you say that I was right, that before you received this order altering your mandate, did you work on any plans relating to such job of yours and such activities bearing in mind that we have here the word "planned"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We made some contingency plans, as it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that two or three days prior to the 9th, you worked on these plans alongside the civilian and military authorities of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you refer to a meeting I had with the Chief of Staff of the 28th Muslim Division, to my knowledge, that was earlier or earlier in the period than two days prior to the 9th. And there we had a discussion with the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, Mr. Becirovic, about what would happen if the VRS would attack the enclave. It's correct. But to say that we made side-by-side plans goes much too far. It was a mutual inquiry over what our point of views were, what would happen if the VRS attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and Mr. Boering were also meeting with the military and civilian authorities of Srebrenica prior to these events to discuss the issue of what would happen in the event of the enclave being attacked?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know of a meeting they had, but it was in the evening or night from the 10th to the 11th of July. And I doubt whether there was another meeting where they discussed technical military business with them. I would have known about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the conflict escalated, the weapons that had been collected and stashed at certain points, were these weapons placed at the disposal of the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you mean the weapons stored in the Weapons Collection Point on the UN compound in Srebrenica, that is correct. They were told that they could pick up their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You no longer prevented them from seizing the weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to look at a document, which is a stenogram of your hearing before the Parliamentary Commission of the Netherlands concerning the Srebrenica investigation, dated the 11th of November, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is document 1D937. Since the document has still not been uploaded into the system - at least not its English translation - we have it in hard copy, and we are ready to make it available to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you the following. Let's look together at the English page 7, the first paragraph. And I would kindly ask for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any reason why, when it does exist, that it's not uploaded yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour. I think there was a technical issue with our profile for uploading. In my knowledge, there is an English translation. And last time I recall we also had difficulty with the English translation. However, for reasons of efficiency and economy we prepared the hard copies, and by your leave, I'd like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask, since when does the English version exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall, Your Honour, last time, when we were leading a witness, we wanted some of the translations excluded. I believe we were told by the Prosecution that there was an English translation, at least in its draft form. However, we were unable to locate it. We have it in Dutch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm greatly surprised that if we have a hard copy of the an English translation here, which seems to be -- I don't know whether it's complete or not, that it could not be electronically uploaded into e-court. That's still -- it's unclear. Mr. Ivetic may have a -- something to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have some more information, Your Honour. It is a problem with the profile for our Case Manager to upload documents into e-court. We can't upload documents in e-court as of yesterday afternoon. The staff of the -- the support staff of the help desk have been informed and have been working on it. We have had continuing problems within the last month with the profile sometimes not working, and that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is important for us to know so that we can urge everyone involved as well to resolve this problem as soon as possible. So it is due to technical problems beyond your control that you were not able to upload it. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll proceed at this moment, although you have not answered yet my question, Mr. Stojanovic, when this translation was available. Whereas, I do understand uploading yesterday afternoon was unsuccessful. But may I take it that it existed for a far longer time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, I'd like to draw your attention to a particular paragraph. In the English version, it is the first paragraph on page 7. You were asked a question and provided an answer. It had to do with the weapons that had been removed and then the BH Army regained control over it. Our predecessors told us that the zone had not been demilitarised. There was a point where weapons were being collected. A place where from the start the Bosnian fighters handed over their weapons. I know that there were some 200 rifles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, where are you reading? The document is not paginated. So I've counted seven pages. I'm at that page. I'm not quite sure I know where you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since it's nearly time for the break, I'll try to locate it exactly and tell you where we are precisely after the break so as not to lose time. In e-court, before we lost our ability to upload it, it was page 7, paragraph 1. In any case, we'll find it in hard copy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break first. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. Could you tell us what Mr. Mladic said aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladic said the following, Miki, which is me, this was a very positive surprise on your part. That's what I could hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should refrain from any comment, positive or negative, anything, during the testimony. And I repeat this. And next time it may have consequences. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, were you able to find the right pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English, it would be page?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be page 7 in our count. Perhaps it's better if you look for number 468, according to the pagination that we have. So I'm quoting for the first passage by Mr. Franken. 468. Thank you. By your leave, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may continue. 468 is, in the hard copy, page 6. And -- on top of that page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 468. Mr. Franken, can we go on. I'll read it out slowly and then I'll put a question. In answer to a question that was put to you, you say: "Our predecessors told us that the area had not been truly demilitarised. There was a Weapons Collection Point which is a place where, from the outset, Bosnian fighters could hand over their weapons. I know that there were approximately 200 rifles. There were also some makeshift weapons and two T-55 tanks. When we took over our duties from DutchBat II, they told us that there were approximately between 4- and 5.000 pieces of weapons in the enclave alongside the people carrying them." My question is this: After this many years, and after additional information you may have obtained after 2002, do you still stand by this assessment of the situation as it was upon your arrival in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, as far as the actual numbers, we still stand to 4 and a half thousand light weapons. And to make an additional remark, we saw in May that there appears a new type of AK47 Kalashnikovs in the area. So I can't say whether that was this addition to the 4 and a half thousand or replacing old ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will have a question regarding that fact. But, for the time being, could we please look at 1D934 in e-court. Mr. Franken, it is a document originating from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are uncertain of its date, but, according to the text itself, in all likelihood, it was drafted following the 18th of January, 1995. That is to say, after your arrival in the enclave. We have a list of weapons, that is to say, pieces and weapons that were handed over. For the most part, it tallies with your assessment. However, when you look at this, would you agree with me that such an assertion is correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you mean that this covers the contents of the Weapons Collection Point, as far as I know, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is why I'm showing this document. It was signed or drafted by Naser Oric. Can we go down the page in the English translation so as to be able to see the last paragraph. It reads, as they are informing the command of Bosnia-Herzegovina: "That UNPROFOR was told that all the weapons had been handed over. Today, however, UNPROFOR representatives are aware that there are armed formations in Srebrenica which have a specific amount of weapons and ammunition at their disposal, and they are trying to disarm our formations and collect all the weapons and they frequently take weapons from individuals carrying them." Does this tally, more or less, with what you included in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It is correct. It is consistent with my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will seek to tender this stenogram report at a later stage because I will still be relying on it when we reach another topic that I wanted to put questions about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can already decide on admission. There is no need to wait until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D934 receives number D277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D277 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have document 65 ter 19425 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, it is an excerpt from an interview, or a conversation you had. Before we look at paragraph 41 of the document, I wanted to ask you something about your penultimate answer. To the best of your recollection, at what point in time did DutchBat observe new equipment and new weapons possessed by members of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That would have been the second half, end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about 1995, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information on how those weapons came into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not actual information. In that period one of my observation posts reported a possible helicopter flight by night. We couldn't -- exactly what was in it we didn't actually see it. It was an observation by -- by the noise. We tried to establish whether it landed, and if, where, by patrols. We found direct -- just hold, eastly of the village of Slatina, and that is in the western part of the -- the enclave. We found a place in the woods over there that was cleared but we couldn't find evidence of a helicopter landing or any signs that -- that stocks were unloaded or whatever. So I didn't have proof of. I just checked whether there was a helicopter, and if, if it had landed. But we couldn't establish that. That's the only information I had about visitors of the enclave, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 41 of this statement, where, inter alia, you say, that you are certain that the ABiH received American weapons. The weapons were delivered in Tuzla and transported further afield from there. Do you stand by this part of your statement you provided?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, it's not a fact. It is an assumption. Because we heard there were landings of Hercules, American Hercules, on Tuzla airport and units, Dutch units there saw big amounts of new combat suits, et cetera, and some time later we saw American combat suits worn by the 28th Division. So that is not a fact. It is a result of analyst -- me analysing some reports. I don't have proof of that and I don't have proof that they were American originated. The suits were of the American type, and I think that's a better statement than saying that it was American equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But if I'm not mistaken, it reads here that you were certain that the weapons were American and that it was not the equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If someone writes "Franken is certain," I am uncertain what this document exactly is. Could you assist us, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my information, this is a debriefing provided by Mr. Franken in the Netherlands on the 31st of March, 1999. Perhaps it would be fair to ask Mr. Franken if he can confirm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you want me to confirm exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether this is a debriefing report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it is without any heading. It's without -- it only says "Interview with Franken." And the date on it is 31st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will conclude with this document with this last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to confirm at the time that the weapons delivered were American?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I said before, it was an opinion, I said it, if you read the text, it -- it looks like if I had actual evidence that the Americans delivered weapons, and that is, in fact, incorrect. As I said before, I got reports so I combined them and took them and analysed them that, through American means, there was equipment delivered to that -- in the end, came into the enclave. But, again, an opinion. I don't have hard proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you about your knowledge of the arrival and landing of planes with weapons at Tuzla airport. What were your sources? And where did you derive that knowledge from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: My sources were Dutch personnel working at Tuzla, at the -- at the staff of Sector North-East. And I derived that out of the phone conversations with those -- this personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no reason for you to doubt that information; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. The facts that has been delivered equipment, et cetera, on the Tuzla airport, I had no reason to doubt that. But, again, I combined other things, et cetera. And my opinion was, okay, I know now where those new combat suits, et cetera, come from. But, again, it was a opinion, an assumption. But for me personally with reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will conclude with the following question. Would you agree that it was at a time when the Security Council resolution was still in place on the prohibition of weapons being delivered in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time to seek to tender this document into evidence although I will rely on it in the continuation of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19425 receives number D278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, I take it that if you do not make a selection out of this document that you consider the whole of the content to be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document has five pages in total, and I will rely on another portion of it. So it seems it would be useful to admit it as a whole. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just to a point of clarification. In the English at least it's only three pages in total, and to the extent it matters, the Prosecution would support the entirety of the document to go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the original is -- let me see. I haven't looked at it yet. Yes, the original is in Dutch, apparently. I don't see a B/C/S translation. Is there any, Mr. Stojanovic? The Dutch version also in e-court at least is three pages only --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and -- yes. But in e-court we have only an original and an English translation. So I don't know where five pages come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in total, it has 43 points that were numbered. So it's only a matter of the number of pages. It is a text ranging from point 1 to point 43, in all three languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My problem is, in e-court, there's no B/C/S version. At least not in my e-court. But in Madam Registrar's e-court, there's no B/C/S version either. So if you're referring to a B/C/S translation, I think it would be appropriate to have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we'll certainly do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, may I switch topics now. I would like to ask you something about demilitarisation. My question is this: Going about your duties that you have described, did you have information that people in the enclave were not only armed but also that members of the 28th Division carried out offensive combat operations outside the enclave deep into the territory held by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Actually there were two occasions reported to me of ABiH actions in VRS territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told that on those occasions there were casualties incurred by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: One of the occasions was a Muslim action north-west of the enclave. I was not told whether there were casualties or an amount -- yeah, I was told there were casualties by Major Nikolic - Major Nikolic being the liaison of the Bratunac Brigade - but not how much. And the second occasion was an action of the ABiH in the area between the enclave of Srebrenica and Zepa, in that area, and he told me then there has been an ambush and six or seven VRS members were killed in that ambush, and the ambush was laid by forces of the ABiH. Further there were all kinds of rumours but never reports and actual knowledge or location or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you may remain seated. If there's any need to consult, you have an opportunity. Please proceed. I think, Mr. Ivetic, that Mr. Mladic would -- briefly would like to consult. And if he keeps his voice at low volume, you have an opportunity to briefly ... Meanwhile, we can continue, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, can you tell me, did you know that, due to the offensive actions carried out by the 28th Division from the enclave, General Smith filed protests with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, requesting that they terminate such a practice?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did not know, but we reported that too in the lines. So it is obvious that they would have taken some action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Can we now look?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry for remark. Just for the record, we protested that with the staff of the 28th Division as well as soon as we got the reports of those two incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter document 17890 in e-court. Mr. Franken, you may not have had an opportunity to see this document. I would kindly ask to you look at it now and to tell me whether you are aware and did you ever had a chance after the events to see this document, which is signed - can we have the next page, please - by Brigadier-General Mr. Nicolai. It's dated the 26th of June. And I'm going to read what it says: "However, I have to inform you that the commanding officer of DutchBat, during the last few weeks, several times had to warn your troops in the enclave to refrain -- restrain from attacks outside the Safe Area. "As you will understand, these kinds of attacks cause responses which endanger the safety of the civilian population in the Safe Area and make it very difficult for UNPROFOR to protect the Safe Area in an appropriate way. "I have to urge you to issue orders to your troops to restrain from this kind of actions." Does this document actually confirm what you said, that this kind of conduct was customary on the part of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I had two reports, a lot of rumours and we even reacted on rumours to warn the 28th Division, so it is consistent with -- with what I said before and with the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But the key reason why I'm asking you is -- by looking at this document is, having in mind that you were in the middle of all these happenings and you were on the ground, would you agree that this kind of behaviour of the 28th Division was in contravention to the law and the obligations relating to demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I see there's an English version in e-court. There's no B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Stewart has just confirmed that there is a B/C/S version and it's not in e-court at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there's no objection against admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objection to the admission. We can assist with getting the B/C/S version uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the translation exists already, then I think there is no reason to MFI. We can just admit in the expectation that the B/C/S version will be uploaded soon. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17890 receives number D279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D279 is admitted into evidence. You may continue, Mr. Stojanovic. But perhaps wait for a second. Yes, we didn't take the pauses we have to take. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have document D17 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's another document, Mr. Franken, produced by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. While we are waiting for it to be uploaded, I'm going to ask you just a couple of questions. Do you know that at one point during those months, a helicopter fell in the area of Zepa, and this helicopter was flying en route to the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know there was a rumour that a helicopter with parts of the staff of the 28th Division in it was down in the area somewhere, not within our enclave. But I didn't know that it was in Zepa. But that was a rumour. I didn't get reports on the UN line or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see Ramiz Becirovic and to ask him whether he was on board that helicopter when it fell down?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had that opportunity, of course. And, as far as I know, not personally but by our liaison, Major Boering, asked him about that helicopter. And, as far as I recollect, he denied that, that things like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you would agree that he had some very visible injuries and that he had problems with the movement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sure. In that same period, Mr. Becirovic asked me whether he could be treated in our hospital because he had some -- some physical problems, and then he said the cause was that he had a fight with the husband of a lady he obviously liked very much. A story like that. So he didn't give the cause that it would have been from the helicopter crash but he had some physical problems and couldn't be treated in the MSF hospital, or in the civil hospital. I consented that. He has been treated in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for one point of clarification. Why if you have a fight with the husband of another lady, why can't you be treated in a civilian hospital? Why did you accept him to be treated by UNPROFOR staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't know the medical details, but as far as I know, he had to be X-rayed with -- on certain places, and hospital in Srebrenica didn't have that kind of X-ray equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was a technical explanation for it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Purely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The activities that you heard of taking place outside the enclave on -- in the territory of the VRS and carried out by the 28th Division, did they have any connection with the order demanding a more active participation of the 28th Division in order to ease the pressure on the Sarajevo theatre of war by tying up the troops of the -- the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Of course, I didn't have any knowledge of an order they get -- the 28th Division got. But it -- it is a possibility. It is a normally military way to ease pressure on other locations by -- by getting offensive on -- in a different area in general. But then again, I never read that order. I didn't have knowledge of the fact that they got that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at the document in front of you and that is the reason I'm asking you this. Look at point 2 relating to a report submitted by the Command of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Actually, the one received by them from the 28th Division, on 23rd June 1995. There is a description of the action takens -- taken deep in the VRS territory. And under item 2, it says, and I quote: "In order to prevent enemy forces from sending additional forces from the Srebrenica and Zepa areas to the Sarajevo theatre, two acts of sabotage were carried out." And here they explain and describe the actions and state the number, as they put it, of Chetniks killed. Does this document refresh your memory by you having received information at the time that these actions were carried out against villages, Osmace and Bijelo Stijenje near Koprivno?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I more or less know the area but I don't know the villages, exactly where they were or where they are that you mentioned. But the statement under number 2 could cope with the report I got from Major Nikolic concerning that ambush and six or seven of his soldiers killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at point 3 now where they repeat, once again, that in order to divert the forces from the Sarajevo theatre and with a view to stretching them out towards Srebrenica and Zepa on the 26th of June, and this corresponds with a letter sent by General Nicolai to the BH Army commander, if you remember, several sabotage actions were taken deep into the occupied territory, 20 to 40 kilometres, covering the municipalities of Han Pijesak and Vlasenica and also mentioned are the village of Visnjica, Crna Rijeka sector, and Vrani Kamen feature. And then it goes on to say in the second paragraph after this one, which is the last paragraph in the English version, it says that: "According to our estimate, more than 40 Chetniks were killed, although we have unconfirmed information that the aggressor lost 71 soldiers." My question is the names of Visnjica, Crna Rijeka, and Vrani Kamen are the names that can jog your memory to the effect that these actions actually took place in those specific areas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If I recollect well, Visnjica was that north-west of the enclave, a village, more or less, west, north-west there. But within the vicinity of the -- of the -- of the enclave at least, and that could refer or be consistent with the report Major Nikolic gave me about that action on a village over there. For the rest, I can't confirm that it actually happened or -- or -- that something happened because I didn't get reports. Generally, it was far out of our line of sight of -- line of observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, is there any dispute about the matters we have discussed over the last five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment to consult, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can just simply say no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, why are we spending -- I take it that if you would have presented this for the bar table and if you would have agreed with the Prosecution that these operations had taken place and were reported at the time, then why bother the witness who is not a personal witness of it? Why bother him with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the main reason I'm addressing this issue is the information that the DutchBat had at the time, in relation to the violation of the demilitarised zone, and without disputing the fact that Visnjica was attacked but the number of casualties is in dispute. My intention was to have a confirmation, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ask the witness about those matters which apparently you consider relevant to be clarified, rather than what you did. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Simply I can remind Mr. Stojanovic and perhaps the Court that it was part of the opening statement that there was a policy of the BiH to attack outside of the enclave to tie down Serb troops from going to Sarajevo. That's part of our case, part of Mr. Butler's case. But it is my understanding that the Defence does ask this testing the credibility of the various parties involved, and that is where it is normally brought up, but it can be overdone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's nice to hear your explanation why Mr. Stojanovic puts these questions, but that's -- My question was whether we are dealing with any matter which is in dispute. Apparently it's not. Mr. Stojanovic, it's not the first time that the Chamber draws the attention to such a fact. Please proceed. Preferably with a matter which is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just finish with this document, Mr. Franken. The name Crna Rijeka mentioned in the document are you aware that that was the place where the command of the Main Staff of the VRS was located?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, that name doesn't ring any bell with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I'd like a brief consultation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, I might use the time for a different matter. I do understand that there is a revised translation for P1421. The Chamber instructs Madam Registrar to replace the old one by the new one. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this document is already in evidence, let me just ask you one thing, if you know, Mr. Franken. Did you have information who was one board of the helicopter that was shot down and whether there were any foreign nationals among them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "no," you mean you didn't have any information? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, you understood me correctly. I didn't have any information about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something about something that you discuss in paragraph 20 of your amalgamated statement, which is P1417. Paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first -- my apologies for intervening. Earlier, Mr. Stojanovic, your questions were about two helicopters. One which may have been there, but we don't know. And the other one which fell down. Now, in your last question, you said it was shot down. And has the witness any knowledge about that helicopter having been shot down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't have any knowledge of the cause of the coming down of that helicopter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently you have reasons to believe, Mr. Stojanovic, although not in evidence, that it was shot down. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I'd like to ask you something about paragraph 20 of your amalgamated statement. Can you tell us, were you involved, directly or indirectly, in the negotiations between the Serb and Muslim sides relating to the supplies of food and other staples to the enclave, as of January 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Of course being DCO I was involved, but not personally. So the answer is: Indirectly, I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian side was prepared to supply food to the enclave on economic principles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The authorities of the enclave at one point, rejected this method of co-operation and trade.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your mind, what was the reason for their rejection of ensuring regular supply of the enclave on business principles? Regular supply of food and other staples?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I never got a reason. Of course, we asked him for it. And if you ask, in my mind, or in my opinion, information we got from other sources indicated that the staff of the 28th Division opposed and that source said that they were themselves involved in the black market and didn't want -- yeah, interference with that. But, again, it's one source, civil source, that told me that, not confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break, let us just focus on the topic of the disarming of the observation posts, UNPROFOR observation posts. Is it true that at one point you received information that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina weren't allowing members of the DutchBat to leave their observation posts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Not only at one point. At many points, they didn't allow us to move the way we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that conduct also contrary to the obligations undertaken by the warring parties with respect to the freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why you, yourself, suggested to the crews at the observation posts not to risk their lives, but, nevertheless, say there and hand over their weapons to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was not the real reason. In fact, the reason was, as you probably know, we had a casualty, soldier, van Renssen, shot by the ABiH. He was a part of the crew of OP Foxtrot retreating from OP Foxtrot, and by experience, I knew that local commanders of the ABiH had their own policies and their own way of acting with -- in spite of what the division said, and since I was in a conflict with an aggressor, being the VRS, and another party locally being just as aggressive towards -- as the VRS, I ordered my soldiers to prevent them from being shot from apparently friendly troops to, Okay, if you don't have an agreement with the local BiH commanders, so not with the 28th Division, the local commander, about retreating, et cetera, then stay on your spot, and if you are surrounded by the VRS, and they want that, then just surrender to the VRS. That's the real reason why I said that, why I ordered them to stay on, if there was no consent with the local BiH commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. I have been waiting for interpretation and it took a while. How did the VRS treat members of DutchBat who surrendered to the VRS at these observation points?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, they treated them in conformity with the rules for that. They treated them correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. None of them was injured or hurt in any other way; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not after they were taken POW by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have in e-court 65 ter document 19423. 19423.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, it is an excerpt from an interview with then-Major Franken at Pleso base on the 22nd of July, 1995, as you can see in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2 in the English, please. The second page in the B/C/S as well. Thank you. One more page in the B/C/S, the next page. One more page in the English, please. Thank you. The second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we are now on the right page, but we shouldn't start -- it's time for a break. We shouldn't start the questions now. Perhaps we deal with that after the break. Could the witness already follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, as far as timing is concerned, are you on track? I think you asked for three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think I'll be even shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave instructions to the Registrar in relation to the translation of P1421, which, by the way, is not there yet, but Madam Registrar is instructed to attach it. Now I'd also like to instruct Madam Registrar that the translation as uploaded until now of D279 will be replaced, or that it can be attached, that is, a translation which is already there but was not yet in e-court. P279 was already admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, before the break, I asked you to look at paragraph 2 of the document. On the 22nd of July, 1995, when describing the fall of observation points, you said: "I instructed them to take as much equipment as possible with them. The BH Army was notified of their withdrawal from the positions but it seems that their internal system of reporting was very poor because that is when the incident with van Renssen took place. It is clear that the BH Army directly opened fire on the observation post from which the crew with withdrawing (see also OPs K, D, U and S)." I'm asking you the following: Which OPs did the BH Army open fire at in the course of those few days? Are those the OPs referred to in this part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I see. As I recollect the BiH opened fire on the crew of OP Delta and then, after that, they blocked them and didn't allow them to take a new position but wanted them amongst the BiH -- in the middle of the BiH position. If I recollect correctly, Sierra came under fire from a direction that we concluded must have been the BiH because there was no VRS elements in that area at that time as far as we know. And it happened also at OP Mike, and that was an observation post in the north-western part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it also one of the reasons why you said that the crews of these OPs should surrender to the VRS and to take with them as many possessions and as much equipment along as possible, as is stated here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, never ordered them to surrender to the VRS. There were conditions for that surrender. That was then when the ABiH withdrew without notification and they were in the open. And in the open, I mean they were surrounded by the VRS. And, yes, I ordered them, as I recollect well, to take as much equipment along as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I seek clarification on your matter. I gained the impression, perhaps wrong, from previous testimony that the incident with Mr. Van Renssen occurred when the crew of the observation post withdrew from the observation post in the direction of the -- the base, of the Potocari -- now I here read in this document: "The BSA entered the OP and requested that the personnel go in the direction of the BSA-controlled area. "Which, I instructed to take with them much as much material and possessions as possible. The BH Army was informed of the withdrawal ... but it seems that their internal communications were poor ..." I gained impression again, perhaps wrong, that it was only after the incident with Mr. van Renssen that you withdrew in the directions of the BSA positions, but then I'm a bit puzzled by when you withdrew in the direction of the BSA-controlled area, that you are still -- or at least Mr. van Renssen was still a victim of BiH shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to clarify that, Your Honour. After van Renssen was killed by the ABiH during the withdrawal, the move that was a consequence of the leaving OP Foxtrot, then the guide-line or the order came to our OPs. As I said before, if you find yourself surrounded, no, withdrawal with the ABiH or not with but at the same moment as the ABiH withdraws from its defensive positions left and right of you, only if the local Muslim commander consents in it. Why? I wanted to prevent that another Muslim soldier shot one of my soldiers. If you find yourself surrounded by VRS, then surrender to them and take as much equipment as possible. Is that -- does that answer your -- your question? We never withdrew in the direction of the VRS. We stayed static until the VRS took over the OP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it's not entirely clear to me. What we have on our screen at this moment is BSA fire intensified. You gave -- permission was given for the post to be abandoned during a break in shooting, but suddenly a T-55 tank appeared and the men remained in the OP. This T-55 tank was whose tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. That was the a tank of the VRS, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this story is only applicable to the events of OP Foxtrot. After van Renssen was killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] to read there. Then it continues, the BSA entered the OP and requested that the personnel go in the direction of the BSA-controlled area, which is opposite to going back to the bases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, nevertheless, which direction did the crew then go? Did they follow this request and did they go in the direction of the BSA-controlled area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not follow that request. They demanded to go back to their base, which was consented by the VRS at that point and then the thing with van Renssen happened when they crossed an ABiH position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now this completes the story. There were some elements missing there at this moment, but it has been clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to move to another topic which has to do with document P1143. Can we, please, have it in e-court. Your Honours, for the record, I will rely on the last document once more, although I could tender it now if you agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, once you've used it, if you -- let's have it. Let's try to avoid any back-log in tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objections in principle, Your Honours. We do note that as the document increase we may at some point need to focus on specific portions rather than have the entirety come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, once a document is in, in its entirety, it is available as a source of evidence for the Chamber, and we will treat it that way. And I think I pointed at that already before. Madam Registrar, it's number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19423 receives number D280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D280 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, before you is a letter sent by the DutchBat commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, dated the 12th of July. We have a description of his meetings with General Mladic on the 11th and 12th of July. Can we look at paragraph 3, please, which reads: "During the first meeting, I have been accused of everything, what happened today, as being the commanding officer of DutchBat. Again, he demanded that there will be no more air strikes and CAS any longer. If air strikes or the CAS should occur or are continued, the Potocari compound with DutchBat members and about 2.500 refugees in it and about 15.000 refugees in the direct vicinity of it will suffer shelling." I'd like to ask you the following first: Did you have any direct knowledge of such threats or warnings being issued to the DutchBat commander at the first meeting, as is stated here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I recollect well, that after two F-16s delivered close air support on the afternoon of the 11th we got by radio a message, and by radio the VRS used one of our armoured personnel carriers and one of our NCOs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, is there any problem with the audio for Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we should fix that first. Problem solved?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we kindly ask Mr. Franken to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sure. After there was actual close air support in the area of the city of Srebrenica on the early afternoon of 11 July, we got a message by radio and used -- one of the radios of the -- our APCs in the hands of the VRS and it was read that message or spoken that message by one of my POW NCOs that close air support had to stop immediately, otherwise the area of the compound and the -- the refugees would be shelled and my 55 POWs would be killed if the close air support didn't stop. So the answer is, or your question, I did have direct knowledge of such threats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although not at that first meeting but through other means, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was before the first meeting took place, Your Honour. The first meeting was in the evening and this message came in the afternoon of the 11th shortly after those two planes did deliver some close air support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the question was about threats expressed during the meeting, but you -- you have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look together at some segments of the first meeting held at the Fontana hotel. Mr. Franken, we have a full transcript of that meeting, and I tried to ascertain whether everything that was said was recorded properly. Did Mr. Karremans at any point tell you that at the meeting there were such threats issued, as specified in this letter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He told me about threats and a threatening situation when he did debrief me when he came back to the compound, that's correct. But, again, I wasn't present, so I can't testify that it was literally what was said or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look together, with your leave, Your Honour -- when I read the entire transcript I singled out certain parts which may be characteristic of that topic. To that end could we please look at P1, which is an excerpt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you already mention it and then I've one question for you. You said you have a full transcript of that meeting. Now I have a vague recollection that at least one of these meetings was not fully recorded. Do you mean that you have a full transcript of what was recorded, or would you say that it was recorded from beginning to end and we have a full transcript also of this first meeting? Just my recollection about which of the meetings was not entirely recorded fails me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was also a point that the Prosecution wanted to say, that there were several -- there was evidence about the extent of recording of these meetings, so that would be a very important point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- if you could point in the evidence to where it is said that the recording and the transcript, therefore, fully covers the meeting, then I would appreciate if you could assist me. But, meanwhile, that is no reason to pay specific attention to specific portions that were recorded and transcribed. So you may proceed but you are invited to assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have a full transcript of what was recorded by camera at the first meeting. So that's an answer to your question. Now, as to whether the first meeting was recorded in its entirety, because we did have testimony about whether everything was recorded at that and the second and third meetings, in any case, I will rely on whatever I have. That is why I would ask to look at an excerpt from the first meeting at the Fontana hotel with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Apologies to counsel, Your Honours. Just one point, it's -- it's not clear from the transcript whether my colleague is contesting whether there is a full transcript -- whether the full meeting was recorded or not. There has been evidence of this, and if that witness was going to be challenged, that should probably have happened then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we rely on the evidence as to whether everything was recorded yes or no. I think that what was recorded was transcribed. And, Mr. Stojanovic, I did not understand the position of Defence to be that every single part of that meeting was recorded but that you have to limit yourselves to those portions that were recorded. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. In that regard, I wanted to say that Mr. Karremans will be the person competent to provide such answers. Can we look at the excerpt P004795. For reasons of economy I want to skip the excerpt that I referred to Ms. Stewart at the beginning, and it is 004745 which is at 00 hours, 49 minutes, 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is it P004795 or is it 004745?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "... you don't need to think. "Of this one at the hotel. "They are here at the hotel. "If you keep bombing, they won't spend time ... utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us look at another excerpt of the same recording from 50:19 to 51:34, which is again Mr. Mladic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "He is one of those who destroyed our dream ... Bosnian Muslims because we were happy country, happy populations, and we had a very good life. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next address by General Mladic is at --

utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you should state first where you stopped. It's now at 51:40:8.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. 51:40, for the record. We will continue at 52:09 to 53:52, where again General Mladic is speaking.

utterances.text: "No, I've been in Lebanon in 1979 as a company commander. I've been in Zagreb in 1991 during the war in Croatia and Slovenia. "So you really came here ...
